title: I Asked 100 Companies for My Data. I Got Deletion Notices Instead
gist: A reporter's attempt to file CCPA data-access requests with over 100 companies repeatedly surfaced misclassified responses (data deleted or opted-out instead of disclosed) at firms like Crunchbase, BeenVerified, and Cash App, and an academic who audited 500+ data brokers found the same systemic pattern, fueling calls for stricter 'data minimization' rules.

insights.claim: Under the California Consumer Privacy Act (in effect since 2020), consumers can request access to, deletion of, or opt-out of the sale of their personal data, and companies have up to 45 days to respond, but the reporter's explicit access-only requests were repeatedly misprocessed as deletion or opt-out requests instead.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Widespread misclassification of a well-established consumer right indicates weak operational compliance infrastructure industry-wide, a latent regulatory and reputational risk for any company holding consumer data.
insights.locator: The CCPA went into effect in 2020

insights.claim: Startup database company Crunchbase permanently deleted the reporter's account after an explicit access-only request that stated 'please do not treat this as a deletion request,' which the company later blamed on a human customer-success 'processing error' rather than an AI tool.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: A concrete example of a data-driven B2B company mishandling a basic consumer-rights request suggests thin compliance staffing/process even at well-known tech firms.
insights.quote: Your account has been permanently deleted from Crunchbase. Please let me know if you need anything else!
insights.locator: One of the first errors came from Crunchbase

insights.claim: Data broker BeenVerified responded to an explicit access request across three separate exchanges by removing the requester's public records listing, phone number, and email from search results and denying identity verification, despite the company stating support agents receive annual CCPA privacy training.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Repeated, not one-off, mishandling at a people-search data broker despite formal training programs suggests training alone is an insufficient compliance control for this industry.
insights.quote: It appears your person report has already been removed from our Person Search results.

insights.claim: Cash App (owned by Block) lists a toll-free phone number in its privacy policy as a CCPA access-request channel, but calling that number resulted in the reporter being placed on hold, told to call the same number again, and asked to call back later so staff could 'understand how to handle' the request.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: A disclosed compliance channel that functionally does not work at a major consumer fintech is a specific, named regulatory-exposure data point for Block.
insights.locator: My attempts to place an access request with Cash App

insights.claim: Elina van Kempen, a UC Irvine PhD graduate and coauthor of a study on data brokers' CCPA compliance, found the same misclassification pattern (access requests answered as deletion or opt-out) after placing requests with more than 500 data brokers, with some brokers never resolving the error.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Independent academic research corroborating the same failure mode across 500+ data brokers elevates this from an anecdote to a systemic industry defect, strengthening the case for regulators to intervene structurally rather than rely on individual complaints.
insights.quote: Sometimes I would make an access request, and the automatic answer was 'We will opt you out' or 'We will delete your data.'
insights.locator: I found solace in chatting with an academic researcher

insights.claim: Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the Consumer Federation of America, called the pattern of misprocessed requests unacceptable and said it exposes the weakness of privacy policy frameworks that rely on companies to self-police in good faith.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: A consumer-advocacy leader publicly framing self-regulation as failed supports the case for more prescriptive privacy legislation, a regulatory tailwind risk for data-broker and ad-tech business models.
insights.quote: That's not an acceptable status quo.
insights.locator: Consumer advocates I spoke with were upset

insights.claim: Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, a law fellow at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said the pattern of noncompliance shows companies are putting too few resources toward ensuring consumers can access their own data.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Under-resourcing of privacy-compliance operations relative to legal obligation is a recurring theme investors should weight when assessing regulatory/legal risk for data-intensive companies.
insights.locator: Experts I spoke with questioned whether companies

insights.claim: Privacy advocates propose 'data minimization' -- limiting what companies can collect in the first place to only what's needed for standard business operations -- as a more holistic fix than the current consumer-driven access/deletion request system, which shifts compliance burden away from consumers.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: A shift toward data-minimization mandates would structurally curtail the scope of data collection that fuels data-broker and targeted-advertising business models, a legislative trend worth monitoring for exposure in that sector.
insights.locator: Both Winters and Tobin-Miyaji mentioned a beefed-up approach
